Based on the healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that structural characteristics of a general practice may not be directly associated with the uptake of an IT innovation in primary care. However, post-graduate education in the relevant clinical condition can play a significant role in shaping its use.

In the case of the diabetes system at our local health department, the findings suggest that practice nurse involvement was crucial in spreading its adoption beyond initial enthusiasm and driving sustained use over time. This highlights the importance of involving healthcare professionals in the design and implementation of IT innovations.

Additionally, research has shown that effective methods for improving adherence to follow-up appointments may be more important than the specific recommendation itself. For instance, reminding patients about their results can be more effective than changing the way follow-ups are recommended.

It's also worth noting that patterns of knowledge and attitudes among unvaccinated seniors may be useful in identifying groups for targeted health messages. This suggests that healthcare providers should take an active role in educating certain populations to improve health outcomes.

In conclusion, while structural characteristics and post-graduate education can influence the uptake of IT innovations, it is likely that practice-specific factors play a more significant role. Further research is needed to fully understand these dynamics and optimize the design and implementation of IT innovations in primary care.
